Quantum entanglement is a physical phenomenon that occurs when a group of particles is generated, interact, or share spatial proximity in a way such that the quantum state of each particle of the group cannot be described independently of the state of the others, including when the particles are separated by a large distance. This means that a measurement performed on one part of the entangled system instantaneously affects the state of the other part, regardless of the distance separating them.

This concept is significant in physics because it challenges classical notions of locality and realism, suggesting that information or influence can travel faster than the speed of light (though not usable for faster-than-light communication). It has profound implications for our understanding of the fundamental nature of reality and is the basis for emerging technologies such as quantum computing, quantum cryptography, and quantum teleportation.
